maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext:
The other night I made an exhaustive analysis of the division that I thought should be made of the county of Brant. I do not propose to add to or repeat that discussion; but I propose to move one resolution, or two, according to the result of the vote in the committee. If the vote is adverse to the first proposition which I shall presently have the pleasure of submitting, it will necessitate my moving a secoud one. The proposition which I submitted the other Mr. DAVIS.
evening, and which I called the city plan, was the proposition of the council and the board of trade of the city of Brantford, as a fair division of the county. In order to show the relevancy of the proposition which I am about to introduce, I may call attention to tbe fact that the committee divided Brant into two ridings, one called Brantford and the other Brant. The facts in regard to the population are these. The plan of the Bill gave Brantford a population of 1,594 over Brant, by adding to the city the west part of the township of Brantford and the township of Oakland. The proposition made to the committee was to make the city of Brantford one riding and the rest of file county another riding, the one to be called Brantford and the other Brant. 1 took occasion to state then, and I repeat now, that under this plan Brantford would of course be much smaller than Brant; but if you omit the township of Tuscarora, which has a population of 3,170, all of whom are Indians, and which has not a voter in it, there would be under the city plan a difference in population between the two ridings of 1,732, making only a difference between tbe two plans of 13S.
1 move that section 27 be so amended that it shall read as follows :
The city of Brantford shall constitute the electoral district of Brantford and shall return one member.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext:
I followed the example of my hon. friend the other night in making my main speech on this question, and I do not propose to take up much time now. In the year 1882, when the famous gerrymander was made by the party opposite, there was no one in the city of Brantford who could be found to assume the responsibility of the injustice that was perpetrated on South Brant by the redistribution of that day. Every Conservative denied having had anything to do witli that scheme. It was born in darkness, but the present larraiiigement thas been discussed in tbe open. Tbe Brantford ' Courier,' tbe organ of the Conservative party, when it saw there was to be redistribution, argued in favour of giving the city of Brantford one representative and the county the other. The city council, in which the Conservatives have the majority just now, passed a resolution in favour of giving the city of Brantford a representative, and at a small meeting of tile board of trade a similar resolution was engineered through. I wrote at once to the city council stating that its scheme was impracticable, that the unit of representation was about 25,000, that consequently, as the city of Brajitford had only 10,000, the thing could not be dong, and that the best we could hope for would be to get two representatives for the county of Brant. That principle was conceded by our friends on the other side, and tbe committee unanimously agreed that the county of Brant should have two representa-

lives. It became then the duty of the committee to divide the county into two constituencies. i What my hon. friend now proposes is to give the city of Brantford, which has a population of 16,619, one representative, and give one to the county with a population of 21,521. Is that right on its face ? Can any one justify one portion of the constituency with 16,000 people being given a representative, while it requires 21,000 people in the other to elect a member ? The only way to bring about equality is to add to the city of Brantford contiguous portions of the comity, so as to equalize the numbers. We therefore add to the city the township of Oakland and that part of the township of Brantford south and west of Grand river. For fifty years West Brantford has been a portion of South Brant. Even the Conservatives, in 1880 and 1890, left West Brantford in South Brant, and in order to increase the number to the proper amount you must add tlie township of Oakland-which cannot be added to North Brant or the county of Brant in any shape-with a population of 785, and that gives 19,867 for the city of Brantford and 18,273 for the county. In other words, the proposition of the majority of the committee, which I endorse, shows a disparity of population of only 1,594, whereas the proposition of my hon. friend from South Norfolk gives a disparity of 4,902. It has always been the intention of tlie House, where there is a disparity in the population, to give the advantage to the rural constituencies, and we have invariably done it. But in this particular instance lion, gentlemen opposite want that policy reversed, and want to give 21,000 farmers the same political power as 16,000 residents of the city. If my hon. friend had been instructed by the Conservatives of South Brant to do the very best he could in their political interests, he would have taken exactly the course he has. There is no other plan you could devise by which you could better promote the political interests of the Conservative party, because in the county of Brant every constituency is Liberal except one, and that is eight miles away from tlie town, and there is intervening territory between them. There is no way of improving the chances of the Conservative party except by adopting the plan of my hon. friend, and that can be his only possible motive. There can be no other. There is no one who wants his scheme except a few Conservative ward heelers. For fifty years Brantford and Oakland have been in South Brant, identified with us politically, and they want to come back again, and we want them. The board of trade are of my opinion. All they wanted was thap the constituency should be called Brantford for commercial purposes. They said : Tack on whatever you like, look to your own political interest, so long as we get the name of Brantford ; that is all we want. Neither did the city
council care. There are only two or three political wire-pullers who want this thing against the manifest wish of the great majority of Brantford and the entire population of West Brantford and Oakland.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext:
Who is C. H. Waterous ?
M. HEYD. He is one of the best friends and political supporters I have. He told me : I do not care anything about the resolution, so long as we get Brantford named as a constituency. I said to him : Did you realize that there was a political wirepuller behind that thing, and that you have been made a tool of? No, he said, I did not -see it then, but I see it now, and if you do what the Tory machine wants you to do, you are a bigger fool than I took you to be. That is his opinion. I do not think that the majority in this House are going to assist the Conservative party to gerrymander the county of Brant a third time after doing it twice. They will require better arguments than my hon. friend has presented.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext:
The course taken by the hon. member for South Brant (Mr. Beyd) makes it necessary that I should speak again on this subject. As we have had a full discussion, it was no part of my wish that further time should be taken up, but it is impossible that the discussion can end here. I simply call attention to the hon. gentleman's course because some hon. members have spoken of gentlemen on this side obstructing the progress of this measure. If that was the object, I am quite as capable as the hon. gentleman is of repeating a speech that I have already made ; but that is not our object, so I shall not repeat myself more than is necessary. It is true the hon. gentleman (Mr. Heyd) has not repeated all his speech, still he has said so much that I should be clearly failing in my duty if I did not deal with what he has said in order if possible to prevent the important city of Brantford being treated unfairly. The hon. gentleman speaks about Tory wirepullers and what they are trying to do. Now, Mr. Waterous is one of the gentlemen who are not satisfied with the proposals submitted here on behalf of the majority on this committee. Mr. Waterous is one of the best known men in Brantford. He is a Reformer, and has been a consistent Reformer all his life. I can tell the hon. gentleman that, notwithstanding the lightness with which he treats Mr. Waterous and those who think with him, he will find that these citizens of Brantford are in earnest. The hon. gentleman talks about Tory wire-pullers having a certain influence in Brantford. I would not say, nor would I allow any one in my presense to say uncontradicted with regard to my own town of Simcoe, that it is controlled by wirepullers on either side. There are as many men in Brantford in proportion to population as there are in Simcoe whom

wire-pullers cannot handle. If there is any wire-pulling or any attempt at dictation, those who are chargeable with it are those behind the hon. gentleman, or else the wire-puller is the hon. gentleman himself, for this is his scheme. The right hon. gentleman (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) when he introduced this Bill, told us that there was no eut-and-dried scheme. And the committee said that they had no figures and no fixed plans. But we find that, even before the Bill was introduced, the hon. member for South Brant wrote to people in the city of Brantford practically dictating what the division should be. I do not think Mr. Waterous will thank him for what he has said1. It will take a good deal to make Mr. Waterous vote against his own party, but I have confidence enough in him to believe that if he is satisfied that unfairness is being practised, he will vote on the other side. The hon. gentleman speaks of this movement on the part of the board of trade being due to the fact that some gentlemen in that body are easily influenced. Now, Mr. Waterous moved this resolution in the board of trade. He is a man who knows something, and one whose actions have some meaning in them. Here is a resolution unanimously passed by the board of trade of Brantford, which, like the board of trade all over the country is a non-partisan body.
At one o'clock, Committee took recess.
Committee resumed at Three o'clock.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: When you left the Chair, I was making some remarks on the change in the form of the riding of Brantford, and was replying to some remarks of the hon. member for South Brant (Mr. Heyd). He was setting out the population according to the Bill, and in his figures he included the Indians in the township of Tuscarora. That is the great point of difference between the plan proposed by the city of Brantford and the plan of the hon. gentleman, which a majority of the committee decided to adopt. I may say in addition, that the city proposition was moved in amendment to his proposition before the special committee to whom this Bill was referred, and it was defeated by a vote of four to three. Now I want to say in regard to the population question that in my view the hon. gentleman was hardly fair in respect to the rule that had been applied by that committee in dealing with an urban population. He said the other night, and repeated to-day, that in every instance the committee had stood by that rule, namely, that an urban population should be larger to entitle it to a member than a rural population. He ridiculed the idea of the city of Brantford with 16,000 asking for a representative, when it would leave a majority in the rural constituency, including the Indians. Now, with the Indians out, the disparity would be no greater than 138.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: [DOT]

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: Why leave them out ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: In the whole township there is not a voter among them, they were deprived of their votes by an Act passed since these hon. gentlemen came into power. The number of voters in the riding of Brantford under this Bill is 1,298 more than under the other plan, though the inequality in the riding under their plan is only 1,594 in population. For the purpose of justifying their argument in respect to population, they put in this whole township. By extending the principle far enough you might have a riding with only half a dozen people in it who are voters, though you might have enough non-voters to come up to the unit. I do not mean to say that where you have a mixed population, where some are qualified to vote and others are not, that rule should not be applied ; but in the territory where the chief body of the people are wards of the government that rule should not apply.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: How many of them ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext:
Three thousand one hundred and seventy. I admit that technically the law says you shall follow the census, but I do not think the law ever contemplated a case like this, and we are supposed to be dealing on a fair principle. I will give you an illustration. We all agree that we ought not to divide a municipality. But suppose a river runs through a particular township, yet it still remains a township, for municipal purposes. So with these reserves, which are outside the municipal law, governed by this government at Ottawa, totally unrepresented in a municipal way, I say it is a distortion of the principle to bring them into the representation. I think therefore that the city of Brantford had a powerful argument in their favour. Then there was another reason. We all know that a redistfibution lasts ten years, and for that reason it is not unfair unless there is a large inequality for people to look a little to the future. I do not mean to say it would justify a change, but keeping within the thirty or forty instances that I can find in the redistributions that have taken place in this parliament, it is not a thing to be laughed at, as my hon. friend did. No doubt he and his friends are masters of Brant. We know it is Liberal, and | I do not think any the less of it. But I do object that, instead of arguing, he merely talks of the people there and tells us that he and his friends are in the majority, and they will be responsible, they will do as they please. Now that is no argument. I hoped from the opening speech of the leader of the government that his supporters, at all events, would discuss matters in a way that would justify the principle that he had laid down.

Now it was known to the members for South Brant that a resolution bad been passed and steps had been taken by the city council to take in the urban population, because Brantford has grown so fast. No one is prouder than I am of the city of Brantford, it is one of our most thriving towns in the west, and the people are enterprising, and I think they ought to take in the urban population. So it was to his own knowledge that they had applied to the provincial authorities to take in these suburbs. Those suburbs were being taken in now, as is proper, not as an attempt to enlarge it for this particular purpose, but because it is an urban population. We all agree in that, notably the hon. member for London (Mr. Hyman). I think it is well to have this urban population, as far as possible, together. This is another of our western towns of which we are all proud. That is, we are proud of it in everything except its politics, on which its people are a little off, but that 'does not prevent them being progressive and enterprising, and western Ontario is proud of such a city. Brantford has taken these steps although they did not have the amalgamation completed before the Bill was framed. The hon. member for South Brant (Mr. Heyd) who represents that city, knows the situation better than I do, and he knows that there is more underlying this action of Brantford than the wish of a few Tory wire-pullers. I believe there is an earnest sentiment there.
I am a pretty hard-skinned Tory, and it Is hard for me to go back on my party, but I say that there are questions on which I would deem it my duty to do so. These people are urban population and their pride is in their city. I think it is well that our centres of population should have that pride and that there should be no jealousy of the larger places, because we want both large and small communities ; they both serve a great end in developing the country, and we all agree that as far as possible in the different constituencies the urban population should be together. I desire to show what was done in Kingston, an exactly parallel ease, except that there the committee took exactly the opposite course. Kingston has a population of something over 17,800, and there as here they added a small rural town or village, the village of Portsmouth, they did what Brantford is going to do, but this only brought the population up to 19,000 odd. The government did not destroy the Reform majority in Kingston by taking Conservative districts from the balance of Frontenac and putting them in the constituency of Kingston to out vote the Liberals in that city ; they put 26,000 in Frontenac, as against 19.000 in Kingston.
I did not bring up this question. I was content to discuss Brant on its own merits, but the parallel of my hon. friend from Brant (Mr. Heyd) was unfortunate. My right hon. friend (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and
the Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick) must have been aware before this Bill was introduced of the intention and the desire of the city of Brantford in regard to this addition to their population, because I have no doubt the petition from the council laid been sent to them, but notwithstanding that they declined to accede to the request, and- therefore I say that it is hardly fair of them to accuse these people in Brantford of being the tools of Conservative wirepullers. Mr. Waterous, the president or vice-president of the board of trade of Brantford, is one of the leading men of that city, and a man whom, apart from his politics, I admire in all respects and his opinion in this matter is probably as correct as mine. It is, at all events, just as houest. The board of trade of Brantford passed this resolution unanimously, after my hon. friend's plans had been sent to them. Papers were sent to me, I presume my information is correct.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: I think I should correct the hon. gentleman there. I do not mind when he varies a little from the fact, but when he says I had written a letter before the board of trade passed a resolution, he is wrong. It was in response to their resolution that I wrote the letter.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: What I intended to say was that before the Bill was introduced the hon. gentleman had written a letter.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: I am much obliged to my hon. friend for correcting me, because I did not know whether the letter was written before or after the resolution was adopted.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: You said the board had passed the resolution after I had written a letter ; in that you were wrong.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: I may have been wrong there ; it is not material to the argument. What I mean to say is that your letter was published in the Brantford papers before the petition either of the board of trade or of the city council was passed.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: No.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: One was passed some time before the other. In any case the right hon. gentleman (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) had knowledge of it before the Bill was introduced, and he took his action after that had been received.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: I think you are mistaken.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: I have the dates, the Bill was introduced on the 31st March.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: In the House ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext:
I think it was on March 22nd that the council passed the resolution, it is reported on the 24th of March.

You deny that they took action before the Bill was introduced, and that your letter was also written before that time ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: I deny that I had written my letter before the board of trade took action.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: I gained knowledge of your letters because they were published in the papers.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: And they were published before one of these resolutions, 1 do uot know which, was passed.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: No, no.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: Before the passing of the resolution of either the board of trade or the city council. The point is that the city council had taken action and that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Heyd) knew of it before this matter was before the committee. There is no dispute between us on this. The hon. gentleman knew of the action of the board of trade and of the city council before the Bill was introduced on the 21st.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: Oh, yes, of course I did.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: And he had written his letter at that time ; that is all I wanted to state.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: You did not state that.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: I state it now, and I say that as I understood your letter was before one of these meetings took place.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: No, no, I deny that again.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: The point is not material, and I accept your explanation.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: Hon. members will address the Chair.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext:
I was addressing the Chair at all times, but I was looking at the hon. gentleman. When I am talking back I like to look back. I say it is not material, but the hon. gentleman admits that he had written the letter before the Bill was introduced and that he knew of the action of the city council and the board of trade. That is all that is pertinent or worthy of discussion. I now propose to read the resolution of the city council which explains the surrounding circumstances. It is thus reported in the ' Courier ' :
It was decided at the meeting of the city council last night to petition the government that Brantford should have a representative of its own. A motion to this effect was brought in by Alderman Wade, seconded by Alderman Westwood. The motion read as follows
Whereas a Dominion census has lately been
^And whereas, the speech from the Throne has announced a redistribution of constituencies for the House of Commons.
And whereas, it has been announced as the government intention to restore county boundaries.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext:
And whereas, to restore county boundaries it will necessitate a change in the present Dominion ridings in Brant county.
And whereas, the municipalities in the county of Brant have for years taken part in the election of two or more representatives to the federal parliament, even when the population was considerably less.
And whereas, the population of the city of Brantford has increased very materially, while other portions have decreased ; so much so that the population of the municipal corporation of the city of Brantford now about equals the whole of the different municipalities forming the county of Brant.
And whereas, the great growth of the city has made it impossible and unjust to return to the old boundaries of North and South Brant, represented by Messrs. Burt and Preston, the population of these ridings being 9,591 and 34,379 respectively, and the average number of votes cast in North Brant is far less than half the number of votes cast in South Brant.
And whereas, this great difference has been largely brought about by the steady and solid growth of the city of Brantford.
And whereas, a redistribution is not made oftener than at intervals of ten years.
And whereas, the city's population is now about equal to that of the other portions of the county, and extensions are about to be made that will largely increase the city's population almost immediately, at the same time diminishing that of the county, making the population of the city in the neighbourhood of 20,000, much larger than the rest of Brant county.
And whereas, other cities with smaller populations have long had representatives of their own.	.
Therefore, be it resolved that this council is of the opinion that Brantford city has now reached sufficient importance, both as to population and otherwise, to have a representative of its own, and that in the redistribution about to take place, Brantford city be made a constituency for the election of a member of the House of Commons, and that a copy of this resolution be sent by the clerk to Sir Wilfrid Laurier, Hon. C. Fitzpatrick, Minister of Justice, Hon. William Paterson, Minister of Customs, and Mr. C. B. Heyd, M.P., at Ottawa, at once, so that they may know the wishes of the city before the proposed Redistribution Bill becomes law.
Alderman Wade, in speaking on the subject, said that in the Dominion there were twenty-seven constituencies with less population than the city of Brantford. Brantford was a city of great importance, it was growing more so, every day, and he thought that it had every right to a representative of its own.
Alderman Harley asked how many cities of equal importance had representatives.
Alderman Wade said it was not a question of cities but of numbers.	.
The motion then carried on the following division :-	_	_r .
Yeas-Aldermen Whitham, Cutmore, Westwood, Wade, Middlemiss, Hartman, Corey, Brewster, Quinlan.-9.
Nays-Harley, Robdrtson, Leitch, Pickles, Turnbull.-5.
Enlarging the city limits.-Prior to the other motion the following resolution was moved by Alderman Wade, seconded by Alderman Corey:- Whereas, our city has been very prosperous. And whereas, our manufacturers have justly met with great success, many of them having

to extend their buildings or move to entirely new premises and erect new plants.
And whereas, the ratepayers of our city have taken great pride in these extensions and have gladly granted different privileges in the extension of fire protection, water mains, exemptions, &c., to very many of these firms with the object of increasing the general prosperity of our city, and largely increasing the demand for all classes of labour including artisans, mechanics, accountants, clerks, stenographers, labourers, and many other in our municipality, thereby insuring work at all times for those herein mentioned, (especially those residing within our city .limits.
And whereas, many of our workmen, mechanics, accountants, clerks, &c., .gladly assist either directly as owners or indirectly as tenants to secure these workshops for the purpose aforesaid.
And whereas, many are now working in our city, residing just outside our city limits, and more houses are being erected for others who have the same intent, all of which .persons, are or will be escaping their fair share of taxation, &c.
And whereas, such a state of affairs is unjust to the city taxpayer, and tends to lessen the demand for houses and lots in the city.
And whereas, our limits are too small for proper growth, taking into consideration our general prosperity, of which we are all proud.
Therefore, be it resolved that this council place itself on record, that it is desirable in the interests of the city that an extension of its limits take place.
The above motion was carried unanimously.
There is a very strong case made out in that resolution. I was more than surprised to-day to see the hon. member (Mr. Heyd) so lightly and-if it is not too strong a word-so flippantly resist this proposal, and make the boast that because he and his friends have a political majority in every municipality, they were going to do as they pleased. If it be true that they have a political majority, why do they insist on being so particular about this ? If I should be so unfortunate as to have this motion defeated in the committee, I will be able to show later on, that the last leg of their argument will be knocked from under. Was it necessary for the hon. gentleman (Mr. Heyd) to make the remarks he did, in view of the resolution passed by the city council of Hamilton and the board of trade of that city. Here we have fourteen aldermen ; nine of them voting one way and five the other, and here we have also the board of trade, unanimously declaring that they make a reasonable request in this matter, and giving us strong arguments why that request should be granted. I do not say that if the wish of these gentlemen were carried out. it would solve the difficulty. Within a few weeks these suburbs will be taken out of the ridings of Brant and put into the city of Brantford, and that would have the effect of tending towards an equalization of the population of the two ridings. There has been to-day a good deal of feeling exhibited with regard to the change in Brant, where the government have chosen to take advantage of their position in a political sense and adjusted that county to suit their own purpose. Now, I am not a prophet nor the son of a prophet, but if hon. gentlemen opposite did not hear from the city of Brantford that they were not Tory wire-pullers who passed that resolution in the city council and in the board of trade, I am much mistaken in my estimate of its public opinion. It is well known that the progressive city of Brantford sends strong men both to its council and board of trade, and I venture to think that they will hardly be flattered by the description given of them by the hon. member for Brantford to-day (Mr. Heyd). We all know that urban populations and rural populations have no desire to be combined in the one organization. In municipal politics, the farming population want to be by themselves and let the residents of the cities look after their own taxation and improvements, and I hardly think it possible that either the city of Brantford or the county will be satisfied with the present arrangement. In my opinion, it is unfortunate that the hon. member for South Brant (Mr. Heyd) that he should take the responsibility of saying that these gentlemen were Tory wire-pullers, and I hope he will regret it politically, though in other respects I wish the hon. member success. It was stated by a gentleman opposite, that the question of voters had nothing to do with the matter. I am quite prepared to concede that there is nothing in the British North America Act about voters, and there is nothing in this Bill about representation by population. The hon. gentleman desired representation by population, but in the division which they make of the ridings under the Bill, the difference in population will be 1,594, while under the plan advocated by the city-leaving the Indian population of Tuscarora out-the difference would be comparatively trifling. I have moved my resolution and I do not wish to discuss the matter further.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: I would like to ask the hon. gentleman whether he would advocate that in the case of the different constituencies where there happens to be an Indian population, the committee should take cognizance of that, and deduct it from the whole population before making the alignment of seats, or does he think that that rule should apply only to the county of Brant ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: I said that it should be done where there was a municipality without any vote in it. It is not necessary to go into a long discussion of any general principle that I might or might not be in favour of. I am not prepared to discuss other cases, because I have not looked into them. It is sufficient, in my opinion, to get this matter adjusted.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext:
These resolutions, passed by the board of trade

of the city of Brantford, reached me ; I think I received them both. They received consideration at my hands, as they merited it, and as all resolutions coming from that body are sure to receive consideration at all times. But the responsibility of determining these matters now rests with parliament, and the views expressed by the board of trade and the city council are considered in connection with the question of the readjustment of the representation of the whole province. Let that be as it may, I cannot assent to the resolution which the hon. gentleman has moved, that the city of Brantford shall be entitled to a member, for many reasons. The hon. gentleman has spoken of Mr. Waterous, an excellent citizen of Brantford, and a member of the board of trade. I would ask the hon. gentleman, through you, Mr. Chairman, who is inciting him to take this interest in the city of Brantford ? Is it Mr. Waterous ? Has the hon. gentleman had any conversation with Mr. Waterous ? Has Mr. Waterous or any other citizen of Brantford written to him or spoken to him and asked him to advocate this ? I want to know. Has any citizen of the city of Brantford urged the hon. gentleman to bring forward this motion, and if so, what is his name ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: The newspapers were sent to me, with accounts of the meetings, and I was asked by the parties writing to present the matter to the House, which I have done with great pleasure, as I will always be prepared to present a grievance of the people.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: I only wanted to know if any one in the city of Brantford or the county of Brant had incited the hon. gentleman to the course he is taking. The argument of the hon. gentleman seems to be that, as there are iu the county of Brant a number of Indians, as there are in other counties and provinces, they are to be left out of consideration in that county altogether. Leaving them out of consideration means that the county of Brant, which is entitled to two members at present, would be entitled to only one ; and I want to know the man who advocates only one member for that county.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman want an answer ? The representatives of the board of trade and the city council wrote to the hon. gentlman himself, Mr. Heyd, the Premier and other members of the government.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: That they only wanted one member ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: That they wanted the city of Brantford to have a member.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext:
I am speaking of leaving out the Indians. The hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Tisdale) is on record as basing his utterances on the ' Cour-Hon. Mr. PATERSON.
ier ' newspaper, which is the organ of the Conservative party in the county of Brant. Therefore we are to understand that, on the advice of that paper, which is the mouthpiece of the Tory party, the hon. gentleman tries to deprive the county of Brant of one of its members in this House. I protest against it. When the population of the province of Quebec is divided by Go to find the unit of representation, the Indian population of that province is included ; yet the hon. gentleman, in the face of that fact, takes a county in another province, where there are some Indians, and demands that they shall be omitted and deprived of representation. I am glad that he speaks as the mouthpiece of the Tory party, referring to the Brantford ' Courier ' as his authority, and I am willing to leave the matter at that. Now, since 1853, when the county of Brant was formed, the town of Brantford, the township of Burford, the township of Oakland, and that half of the township of Brantford lying south and west of the river, constituted the riding of South Brant, Tuscarora being omitted. Under the gerrymander pei'petrat-ed in this House in 1882, the townships of Burford and Oakland were taken out of South Brant and thrown into the adjoining county of Oxford ; but even under that gerrymander the south half of the township of Brantford was left in the riding of South Brant, along with the city of Brantford. We have brought back the townships of Oakland and Burford into their own connt.v; and if the city population had not grown in greater proportion than the rural population, these townships would have been put in South Brant, which I dare say would have pleased their people. But in that case the inequality between South Brant and North Brant would have been very great-so great as to make that division impossible. Therefore, the simple solution was that the township of Burford, having between 4,000 and 5,000 souls in it, instead of being attached, ns formerly, to the city of Brantford and the south riding, should be attached to the north riding, nearly equalizing the population. The county of Brant into two ridings, to be called respectively the electoral district of Brant and the electoral district of Brantford.
(a.) The electoral district of Brantford shall consist of the city of Brantford and that part of the township of Brantford north and east of the Grand river.
(b.) The electoral district of Brant shall consist of the townships of Onondaga, Tuscarora, Oakland, Burford, South Dumfries, that part of the township of Brantford south and west of the Grand river, and the town of Paris.
For the information of the committee, I produce a plan, to show that the division I now propose is much better than that proposed in the Bill, both geographically and with regard to the contiguity of the different portions of the respective ridings to each other. The Bill proposes that the township of Brantford shall be projected

like a wedge into the centre of the riding of Brant, separating the township of Bur-ford from the other parts of the riding with which it is connected. I was very glad to hear my hon. friend from South Brant say that he wanted equality of population, and also that the city of Brantford should be in as close association as possible with the rural part of the constituency. My proposition would place the city with that portion of the township of Brantford on the side of the river to which it belongs ; for, as some hon. gentlemen have said, we must consider the river as the dividing line, not for municipal purposes, but for electoral purposes. Therefore I put the hon. member for Brant on the horns of a dilemma; he must either accept my proposition, or confess that he was insincere when he spoke of the importance of equality of population and of the city being in close association with the rural part of the constituency, which is contiguous to it. I have to abandon the city proposition for the present, because it has been voted down. I am retaining the Indians as part of the population, and the result is that there is only a difference of twelve in the two ridings under the plan I now propose. My proposition gives you more compact and convenient ridings. It is not the fault of the ridings that the county of Brant was originally laid out in the shape it has. The counties of Ontario were not laid out at all with the idea of forming voting constituencies. Many of them were laid out, as in northern Ontario to-day, before there was any population in them. In those days, away back about 1800, the constituencies were laid out without reference to appearance, but solely with regard to association, and that is the reason why, in many ridings, if you stick to county boundaries, the shape will be worse than if you had laid them out without reference to those boundaries. The only explanation for the plan laid down by this Bill is for the purpose of giving 230 Liberal majority outside the city of Brantford instead of 100, as would be the case under the plan I offer, and making the consituency safe, if the city should become Conservative, which has hitherto been considered doubtful.

It is six o'clock, but I shall finish in a few minutes, if hon. gentlemen will bear with me. I intend to quote from the Toronto ' News.' I shall not quote the figures given by that journal, but I will give the reference to the date of issue, so that any hon. gentleman can consult the figures. As I have said, I quote this journal with all the greater confidence, because nobody will say that it is a Conservative paper. Its statement of figures is au honest, straightforward statement, and it covers the point referred to by the Postmaster General. The following is

the quotation to which I have referred, and it will be found in the Toronto ' News ' of July 25th, 1903 :
The 'News' presents herewith a table showing how the votes polled in Ontario in the last general election, of 1900, would have resulted had they been counted, not in the constituencies arranged by Conservatives in 1892, but in the constituencies arranged by a Liberal majority of the Redistribution Committee of 1903.
The table is the result of an examination of the whole list of Ontario constituencies, except the Torontos, Algoma, East and West, Nipis-sing, Rainy River and Thunder Bay, none of which can be calculated upon the now available data. It shows that in the districts thus canvassed the Conservative majority of 16 would have been turned into a Liberal majority of 15. This is done without the change of a single voter's opinion, simply by the .process of counting the same ballots in different groups. The net gain to the Liberal representation is eleven, and the net loss to the Conservative representation, twenty. The table shows a decrease of nine in the constituencies, but this is reduced to six for the province at large by the creation of a new Toronto member and the increase in the representation of New Ontario.
The process followed in compiling the table has been simply to subtract from the total party vote of the old constituency the party vote of those sections which it is to lose, and to add the vote of those sections which it gains. The result on the representation at Ottawa is shown in the columns on the right, where the figure under the word Liberal indicates the effect on the Liberal representation, a (1) if it be a gain, and a (-1) if it be a loss ; and similarly the Conservative gains and losses under the Conservative heading. A constituency taken over, as Brockville for example, from one party to the other, appears in both columns, as a plus in one and a minus in the other.
All the constituencies in which any change has been made appear in the table, except the incalculable ones mentioned above.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I was under the mistaken impression that the House was going .to adjourn at six o'clock, and for that reason I drew my remarks to a close, although I had not concluded what I desired to say. I may say to the hon. Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick) that since six o'clock I have corrected those mistakes in the tables of population which he gave, so that the figures in regard to the fifty-one constituencies which I enumerated will be correct, even in the unrevised ' Hansard.' I wish to draw some conclusions for the committee from the figures which I have submitted, and to show that the principle of representation by population lias not been by any means uniformly applied, and I trust that the right hon. the Premier and his colleagues, who are responsible for this legislation, will reconsider it as a whole. The figures which I Hon. Mr. TISDALE.
have submitted show that if forty-six constituencies, which I have named, were all to elect representatives from one party, then a population less by 133,000 than half the whole population would be able to elect a majority of six members to this House. Surely it is fair to ask the government, in such a case, to pause and consider the result of the application of such a principle or to reconsider the way it has been applied. To give a still fairer illustration, I added five constituencies, making a total of fifty-one, and laid before the committee the, to me, monstrous proposition that, under the principle of manhood suffrage, fifty-one out of the eighty-six representatives would be elected by an average population of 21,115 each, and that the other thirty-five would require a population of 31,325 each. This, I submit, is a startling proposition. Hon. gentlemen opposite are responsible for the introduction of manhood suffrage in Ontario as distinguished from the property qualification which had previously prevailed, and I admit that the Conservative party rather clung to the property qualification. Manhood suffrage, as contra distinguished from property qualification, means one man one vote, that one man is as good as another. In the first redistribution, in 1872, Sir John Macdonald adopted as his first principle representation by county boundaries as far as practicable, the same principle that the right hon. leader of the government and the Reform party are standing by to-day. But there was this difference, that we, in 1S72, took over the franchises of the old provinces of Upper and Lower Canada ; we had property qualification of a very substantial nature ; we had votes by townships, one list being prepared for a whole municipality ; we had ex-officio county officers as returning officers and deputy returning officers, and the entity of a county which was to be represented was more of a representation of property, because we had multiple voting. What I mean by that is that in every riding where a man had a property qualification he could vote, and thus the representatives in those days represented more the property, which was an old Tory proposition. Many of us Conservatives of to-day admit that we went too far in those days. How was that met in 1872 by one of the straightest and ablest and wisest of Reform leaders, Hon. Alexander Mackenzie? He moved that the rule should not (prevail, that there should be representation by population. The Reform party, before and since that day, or at all events up to 1899, stood by that principle, and I remember well the] agitation!, particularly in in 1872 and up to 1882, for 'rep. by pop.' The old Reformers stood up for that principle of representation by population, and I am willing to allow them whatever credit they deserve for securing the success of

that principle. In 1882, Sir John A. Macdonald changed his base, and the Conservative party is responsible for his change of base. He said :	The feeling in favour of
representation by population is growing ; the property franchise has also been much lowered or extended. In 1885 he extended that principle still further. In 1882 the Reform party did not go back on the principle of representation by population, but they claimed the Conservative party were taking advantage of it unduly to interfere with county boundaries to their detriment, bijt I did not understand the Reform party at that time to abandon the principle of representation by population when it came in conflict with county boundaries.
Then we came to 1892. I took part in the debates on the redistribution of 1892. I have always tried to stand up and assume responsibility for a principle, and I am prepared to say that in no country in the world has there been a fairer distribution than was made in 1892 in the province of Ontario. So under all the circumstances, I am proud of the part that I took. I am standing up here ten years afterwards, to be held to account for the speeches I made. They were not long, and I think they were to the point. We stood up then again for representation by population, without any unnecessary interference with county, municipal or city boundaries. The number of representatives in Ontario was the same as before. As I grow older and feel my responsibilities more, I become less anxious about what my party thinks of me, and a little more anxious about what the country thinks of me; because I begin to think that my time is short, and I want to leave a record in the history of my country above all party questions. I say then that at that time we had to do what most parties have to do. We had to give Toronto one member more on account of its great growth in population, and we had to give a member to Nipissing, a district of fiteen or twenty thousand people, that had none. We made as little disturbance as possible in the province of Ontario. Without my advice-I mean that I was no more than an ordinary private member, I was only a short time in office-without my advice they decided to wipe out two ridings in the Niagara peninsula. The Niagara peninsula is very dear to me, because my county is there. They disturbed nothing except the Niagara peninsula. They cut two ridings off in that oldest and most historical part of the province. They cut out one of the ridings of Wentworth, held by a Reformer, Mr. Bain, a fine man, a great friend of mine, who made an impartial Speaker, so far as his light went. No man on either side ever had any cause to complain. He was respected on both sides of the House, and by both parties in the country. They cut out Monck. whicii was a Conservative constituency, held by Mr. Boyle, and it disappeared from the slate. They distributed most of the population of the two ridings cut out between the old ridings of Lincoln and Niagara and Haldi-mand and Monck, which was represented by my good friend Mr. Gibson, who has since been raised to the Senate, an honour of which he is worthy ; and we gave Dr. Montague from 250 to 300 majority, and we gave Mr. Gibson 500 majority as parties were then. But the hon. member (Mr. Lancaster) now representing the constituency, took away that large majority from Mr. Gibson, and my friend, Col. Thompson, to my surprise and the surprise of both parties, left the Hon. Dr. Montague at home. That shows, at all events, that nothing that is done with a constituency in this House will, in a certain sense, prevent the people from expressing their will at the polls. I myself was not, in a political sense, -what might be called well treated in that redistribution. It put on my riding a township with a population of 5,000 from the adjoining county of Haldimand, and that township gave a majority against me, on the two occasions in which I have since been a candidate there. However, the principle adopted in the redistribution of 1892 was applied to all the constituencies touched, and in that respect it was fair, and in that respect it differed from the principle now applied by the government. The figures which I have given this afternoon show the startling result, from a political point of view, of the redistribution proposition now submitted by the government. I ask the consideration of the House to these figures. I want to say here that no party could make a fair redistribution of the population of Ontario on the principle of comity boundaries which this government lias adopted. As to urban population, I believe In the English plan, of giving it distinct representation as far as possible. This plan now proposed by the government cannot work out in a fair manner, when you give to one constituency with a population of 35,000 a representative, and when in another ease you give a constituency with 13,000 a representative. I refer to the county of West Northumberland, which has a population of 13,055. Such a plan as that will never satisfy the people of Ontario. For my part, I do not wish to be throwing stones at my opponents, and I certainly do not forget that we ourselves have done things which placed our opponents in a very good position to throw stones at us. I sincerely and honestly believe that if the Prime Minister had made a proposition for a conference instead of sending the Bill to a committee a fair redistribution would have resulted, and I cannot conceal my great disappointment at the result. Let me refer for a moment to the county of Norfolk. I was born in that county, and I have a great regard for it. Norfolk was in the van of the development of this country. It was settled

between 1700 and 1800, long before there was any settlement west of the St. Lawrence river except Niagara, then called Newark; long before there was a house In Toronto, and long before the city of Hamilton, now represented by two members, was ever heard of. Norfolk is a county of old associations, but Norfolk has not grown in population as other places, and even to-day the county town has only about 3,000 inhabitants.
We feel strongly that we are entitled to consideration in the redistribution. I have told you that while Walpole went against me, Norfolk upheld my position in 1892, when I imperilled my political life by standing up for a fair representation by population. At the same time, we retained our two representatives. I say that any system of representation that unnecessarily or unduly reduces the representation of the older parts of Ontario ought to be and will be resented by the people of those districts. The present residents of Norfolk and their forefathers have for a hundred years or more been paying taxes and doing service for the country. They came to Ontario a hundred years ago or more, when a great part of the province was unknown, long before the red man had disappeared and when there were but few neighbours. Those people came there, why ? Because they had been driven there by the American revolution-many of them from wealth and affluence, and many of them in distress because they could not stand the treatment that the colonists of that day saw fit to mete out to those whose rights of property and liberty of person had been guaranteed to them by solemn treaty, and the laws of nations and civilization, but matters became, as we all know, so intolerable, they had to leave. Among the descendants of these men have grown up great political questions. They did not perhaps know as much as we do about the principles of government, but they had their own views, and their different views, and they expressed them strongly. But they stood together when trouble arose and when the country required their services ; and I say that they will resent any interference with their political or representative rights. I do not care what principle of a political nature you propose to apply to this matter ; I say you ought to leave alone, as far as possible, the representation of the older political districts of the province of Ontario ; and I have a proposition to move which will indicate a way of doing that on a fair basis. I want to say more : you are interfering seriously with the Niagara district, and I want to stand by that district regardless of politics. We have our disagreements politically, and we argue them out good natured-ly ; we get warm over them, because we are sincere ; but when the political fight is over, we are good personal friends. Once or twice, when matters from outside, since my time, Hon. Mr. TISDALE.
came very near to bloodshed, we stood in the ranks. Reformers and Conservatives alike prepared to fight as our forefathers and had actually stood and fought to the death in early days in Norfolk, and we will stand together in the ranks politically, if necessary, to defend our rights in connection with this question. Now, the peninsula of western Ontario is composed of five counties-Norfolk, Haldimand, Welland, Lincoln and Wentworth. Out of these five counties two constituencies were taken by the redistribution of 1892. It was explained that this would disturb the representation of the whole province 'the least of any other' possible plan, and that explanation was accepted by the people as satisfactory. The redistribution was applied fairly, as I have explained ; I am proud to be able to say that. In the figures I give, I might take South Norfolk alone, though my case is stronger with North Norfolk added, and my motion of course includes both - Norfolks. The population of Norfolk county is 29,147 ; Haldimand, 21,233 ; Welland, 31,588 ; Lincoln, 30,552 ; Wentworth, 26,818 ; making a total of 139,338 ; an average of 27,867. If you add one riding to that, it will make the average 23,223 to each of the six, which is nearly the average of the rural constituencies. If you compare it with the average of the fifty-one constituencies I have mentioned in which you will have, if they go one way, a majority of sixteen in the eighty-six constituencies, you will have for each of the six the average of the fifty-one and 11,940 of a surplus. Now, I propose to move that these five counties be so redistributed that they shall have six ridings instead of five. I presume that our protests on this subject will be heard, because we are in earnest in making them; and if we weary hon. gentlemen opposite, we do so- and in saying this I think I speak for everybody on this side-in a cause which we think we ought to represent.
It is always rather discouraging to know that however much work you may put into a proposition if the party in power says nay you can only appeal from their decision to the masters of the administration, the people of this country, but all parties will have to put up with whatever they may decide. But when we are confident of being right, though defeated, we have preserved our honour and self-respect. I certainly feel personally aggrieved at the load which is being put on the Norfolks, particularly South Norfolk. The two Norfolks return respectively a reformer and a Conservative. But let me say that both ridings were happy and content as they now are, and have raised no cry for county boundaries. When one of the townships of Haldimand, with a population of 5,000, and which gave a majority against me, was added to South Norfolk, there was no outcry. The people had known me from my boyhood and though at first some were inclined to resent the

*change and were disposed to hold me responsible, when I explained to them that it was not done at my solicitation and that by this change the government were giving the unit of population-because previously I only represented 17,000 people-their resentment disappeared, and I am glad to say that the majority in that particular township was less against me in 1900, when we had a harder fight, than it was before.
I do not like the disturbance or extinction of old associations, I have been here some sixteen or seventeen years, much longer than I ever thought I would be here; and I do not believe that I would have been induced to try and get here if I had anticipated so long a term. And the only thing under heaven that would induce me to try and get here again, is the fact that you are trying to impose on my people. As 1 have said, they are satisfied as they are in both ridings. And let me tell the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton), if he thinks he will have a walk-over in the next election, he may be * mistaken. There will be somebody in the field against him, whether it will be myself or some one else. There will be somebody to represent the feelings of the people, which I am endeavouring to express here to-night. When the change was made in 1892, the party I supported was in power, and as I had some influence at that time, representing so close and difficult a riding to carry, if I had raised my voice against it, I believe I could have prevented the change. But I said, no, it is a fair thing, under the principle you are adopting, do not mind me or South Norfolk, we will stand by the principle you have adopted, and take our share of the whipping, if necessary, rather than not do what is fair. What is the case now ? Let me cite in particular four ridings that are smaller than Norfolk. The smallest county, Northumberland West, has a population of 13,048 ; Prince Edward Island, 17,864 ; East Peterborough, has 16,299 ; and North Middlesex, 16,419. Three of these are Liberal constituencies, Norfolk is to have 29,147. There are sixty-eight out of eighty-six constituencies that are smaller than Norfolk, and yet we can only have one member. The city of Toronto was included in the larger ones, having over 40,000 for each of its representatives. I protest against the representation of Norfolk being lessened. It has many claims for consideration. It has two members in the local legislature, both Liberals. I am not afraid for my party against any Liberal in South Norfolk, which, even as it is under the Bill, if it stood alone, would have a population of 20,000. But I want North Norfolk to be treated right as well. My motion will keep both North and South Norfolk in existence. If it will not tire the House, I would like to read a short extract from my remarks in this House in 1900, when the Minister of Customs attacked the redistribution of 1892. I said :
As hon. gentlemen opposite, especially the hon. Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) have seen fit to attack the redistribution of 1892 so strongly, and as other branches of this subject have been fully discussed on both sides of the House, I propose to detain the House for a short time to say a few words in regard to the redistribution of 1892. I am especially surprised that the Minister of Customs should attack that measure, because I say without fear of contradiction that the redistribution, it effected, w>as as fair as it was possible to make it, and was perfectly equal in its political effect. It was felt, and it is beyond question, that Toronto was entitled to at least one additional member. It was felt also that Nipis-sing, where there were thousands of people without representation, should he represented, and, therefore, to make two mew constituencies it became necessary to abolish two old ones. What did we do 7 We took Niagara peninsula and we made Lincoln county for my hon. friend who mow represents it, that If he had not got that help, he would not have bad a seat In the House in 1896, because if the constituency remained as it was before then, he would have been defeated. We put Monck with Haldimand and made it stronger Conservative and we abolished Monk held by a Conservative and North Wentworth held by a Reformer. We put the township of Walpole in South Norfolk, which equalized the population, because South Norfolk only had 17,000 before, and we made It 22,000. Walpole was, and iis a Reform township and it gave a majority against me in 1896. If a fairer Redistribution Bill could have been made, as far as Ontario is concerned, I would like to know how. If; therefore, hon. gentlemen opposite cannot find stronger arguments to attack the Redistribution Act of 1892, I only hope they will pass a Bill that will be as fair, when the opportunity is given them. We have heard many reasons urged in support of the changes now proposed, but no one can contend that this Bill, with the facts badly stated, can show as fair a redistribution as the Act of 1892, with regard to the province of Ontario.
If the record of hon. gentlemen opposite, when this Bill goes through, is equal to our record in regard to the redistribution of 1892, we shall have no reason, fti my opinion, to complain. Now, if the committee will listen a little longer, I should like to give some account of Norfolk historically. I could quote a great deal, but I do not wish to weary the House or overload ' Hansard.' Let me give simply a few brief extracts from the historical record of Norfolk, to emphasize the facts many of which I have within my own knowledge. I have made the following brief extracts :
It was first settled during the last ten years of the century before the last, that is between 1790 and 1800.
Practically the United Empire Loyalists and British emigrants, who came to America at the close of the struggle which severed the thirteen colonies from the British empire, were the founders of Norfolk-the former class had sacri- * ficed their homes, their wealth and in many cases their lives in defence of British connection.
Now, I read the next paragraph with due modesty. It speaks of the forefathers of myself and others. But I confess that, for

myself, I have never been able to live np to the lofty example set by the lives of these noble men, nor would 1 compare myself with them for a moment. Memory, going back to near the beginning of my sixty-eight years of life, gives me glimmerings of the hardships which these distinguished patriots endured, endured cheerfully in order that they might bring up their children in the enjoyment of the blessings and opportunities of a better civilization than that which was possible in the days of the earliest settlement:
They were as a class pre-eminently distinguished by honour and industry-their example of thrift, honesty and unswerving loyalty has been of vast benefit to Canada. A .large population of early settlers of Norfolk belong to the best families of this class. They had held high positions in the army during the war of the revolution.
At the time Norfolk was first settled Newark (now Niagara) was the only important village west of the St. Lawrence. Toronto had not a single house built about 1794 ; Hamilton had no existence ; the first in Brantford was built in 1806. The counties to the east and west of Norfolk had not a single settler.
Courts were established there for the London district before 1800.
The Norfolk -militia were on service from 1812 to 1815 and took part in most of the stirring scenes of those years. Happily there was little bl-ood shed within the border of the county, but at the taking of Detroit, the battles of Port Erie, Lundy's Lane and Queenston Heights, the Norfolk soldiery did honour to the sires from whom they sprung.
The first Canadian parliament sat in 1792. The first election of whieh we have any account was held in 1800. David W. Smith was the name of the member elected and became Speaker of the House.
I knew tbe family well. They were solid old-fashioned Reformers, but none the less respected by the descendants of the strong, old-fashioned Tories of the early days.
Not to add#more at present, though possibly there is much more that I may say at another time, should occasion arise, I might suggest to the right lion. Prime Minister that, as it is nine o'clock and Friday night we should adjourn. But I will conclude my remarks on this motion, and submit the amendment that I have to offer, if the right hon. gentleman wishes. I have spoken without preparation. Whether I have spoken wisely or eloquently, at least I have expressed the views that I honestly hold, and the sentiments which actually move me. I thank the House for their kind attention and the interest they have shown in what I had to say. This is not with me a mere question of politics. We are dealing now with a constituency which is my home, whose people I have known all my life and whose history for many years is with me a matter of personal recollection. And if I am affected by the memories which a 'discussion of this kind suggests, I can only say that I am one of those who believe that he is something less than a man who would Hon. Mr. TISDALE.
not he affected by the consideration of matters so intimately associated with that part of his country which is peculiarly his home. Perhaps X should feel sorry, even though my age might seem some excuse, to exhibit any signs of being affected even by the consideration of questions so laden with personal memories. I conclude, Mr. Chairman, by placing in your hands the following amendment:
Whereas, in fifty-one constituencies in the province of Ontario, as proposed by tbe Bill whieh had the least number in population, the average population is 21,115 ; -and whereas, the population in tbe proposed five electoral districts of Norfolk, Haldimand, Welland, Lincoln and Wentworth, excluding Hamilton, amount to 139,338, in the Bill, thus requiring for each of the five districts an average representative unit of 27,867. Therefore, this committee is of the opinion that the said last mentioned districts are entitled to a representation of six members and that the schedule should be revised and amended accordingly.

speechtext: This amendment is out of order and cannot be received except by consent of the committee. It is not relevant to any section, and if it were adopted it could not be included in the Bill.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: It seems to me, without questioning your ruling, that this might still have a reference to section 14. However that may be, we would have some observations to offer upon the amendment which my hon. friend from Norfolk has made. He has coupled with it a suggestion that possibly the House would suspend consideration of this subsection. I would ask my right hon. friend to accept tliat suggestion. We might take up some other sections and leave this one in abeyance, with the motion which refers to it, and upon which we would like to offer some observations ourselves.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext:
It is rather late In the day to take up tbe time of the House in discussing whether we ought to adopt the principle of county boundaries in redistributing the seats. But I must remind my hon. friend from Norfolk that I think he and his party are responsible to a great extent for the" adoption of that principle. I cannot agree with him that there was no cry in the country, to use his own words, for some different principle from that which was adopted in 1882. My hon. friend has quoted a lot of figures to show the political results that would exist from the redistribution in the proposed Bill. My hon. friend and the members of this House on both sides are too well acquainted with the various constituencies to place much reliance upon the figures that have been quoted. If they show anything, they show the political injustice done to one party under a former redistribution, which is now being remedied to some extent. I am willing to admit that there may be a great deal said pro and

con as to whether the principle of county boundaries is the best method of creating seats for representation in this parliament. We must all admit that great inequalities of population are inevitable, but it is rather late in the day to question this principle now. Parliament appointed a committee to arrange these constituencies within county boundaries, having regard as much as possible to representation by population. Why do I say that the Conservative party are responsible, more, perhaps, than the Liberal party, for the adoption of this principle ? Because in the redistributions of 1882 and 1892 they laid down as a reason for departing from municipal boundaries, especially in the province of Ontario, their desire to equalize population. At that time a Bill was introduced departing altogether from the principle that had been accepted as the governing principle. It was pointed out that injustice was being done to the people of this country from a political standpoint. I wish to quote from a pronflnent member of this House at that time a warning that he gave to the government of that day. He was a prominent supporter of the government at that time; I refer to the late Mr. Dalton McCarthy. I will read a quotation from his speech made, in 1892, which will be found in the ' Hansard ' :
Now is the time to do what is right ; and if the House does what is right on this occasion, I believe it will be impossible for any party-even for my hon. friends opposite iii whom I have not as much confidence as I have in the party I support-should the occasion arise, to do what is wrong. But X agree in what the hon. member for Queen's said, that if they ever get the chance they will be perfectly justified in introducing such a gerrymander as will keep us out, so far as they can, from political life for twenty years. They will he perfectly justified in doing that. I mean to say that if we continue the system which exists, we cannot expect, when the other side get in, as they may, that they will do otherwise. Surely it cannot be that we have the right to cut up the constituencies in order to gain party advantages, and howl at the other side, when they get In, for doing the same.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman say that the late Mr. McCarthy was a supporter of the government at that time?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: He says so in the speech from which I have quoted.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: Every one knows that he was not.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext:
I might not have referred to him as a supporter of the Conservative government had he not stated in his own speech that he was so. At any rate, he was for a long time a supporter of the Conservative government, a member of this House, and one of the ablest lawyers in Ontario, if not in the Dominion, a gentleman who took a very high position in many public matters. Now, 349
I think if my hon. friends opposite win lay aside for a moment their strong partisan feeling, they will acknowledge that the Liberal party have refrained from doing as Mr. McCarthy suggested they would do. If my hon. friends had felt the responsibility wiiieh the hon. member for South Norfolk (Hon. Mr. Tisdale) now says he feels, in departing from the principle of county boundaries and adopting another principle, had adhered more closely to the principle of representation by population, had not committed such an injustice to the people of the country as between the political parties, there would be a stronger support for his suggestions than there can be now. My proposition is that the adoption of the principle of county boundaries is the best remedy that has been suggested, and if my hon. friend expects to get support in this House for some other principle, he will have to show that it would work more advantageously and more justly. I want to point out to fny hon. friend, and I think I can prove, that there was a very much greater departure from the rule of representation by population in 1892 than there Is at the present time. I shall prove this to him by taking three constituencies, Simcoe, Toronto and York, and giving the population that they had under the Bill of 1892. These populations were as follows :

South Simcoe	 20,824
East Simcoe	 35,801
Toronto, West	 73,827
Toronto, Centre	 26,632
Toronto. East	 43,564
North York	 20,264
East York	 35,148
West York	 41,857

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: Would my hon. friend give the unit of West Toronto ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: I am giving now the constituencies.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: The hon. minister knows that West Toronto with a population of over 70,000, has two members.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: Certainly. Would my hon. frieud give the total population of West Toronto ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: I will find it for the hon. gentleman, I have not it here, I think it was 144,000 if my memory serves me right.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext:
I will leave that out of consideration because perhaps the hon. gentleman does not see the point I am trying to make, that while it was declared that the principle of representation by population was given as a reason for departing from county boundaries, I want to show how it worked out and to compare it with the three constituencies in which the largest differences exist under the present Bill. In Simcoe there was a difference of 14,977 and between the two constituencies in Toronto which were repre-
