seated by a single member each there was a difference of 16,932.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: Were these constituencies changed in 1892 ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: They were changed in 1882 or 1892.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: What change was made V

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: They departed from the principle of county boundaries both in Simcoe and York.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: I would be very sorry to accuse the hon. minister of doing anything that would not become a gentleman, but he has given the population of these ridings for 1892 whereas, if I understand rightly, none of these constituencies were interfered with then except West Toronto, -which was given another member. The hon. minister, to be [DOT] fair, should give the population in 1881.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: Were the constituencies to which the hon. minister referred interfered with in 1892 at all.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: They were interfered with in 1882 when the redistriuution took place.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: The figures which have been given were taken from the census of 1892.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: There may have been a slight difference, but it would be very slight, in the population of that year and that of 1882. I shall examine the figures and see what the difference was. If there was any difference I shall be glad to give the Committee the figures from the census of 1881.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: May I say to the hon. minister that I cannot understand his line of argument because he is speaking of several of these constituencies as they were in 1892, but there was no redistribution in that year except in the case of Toronto, for that reason I cannot understand why the argument should apply.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: I always understood that there was a redistribution in 1882 and if these figures were out of proportion in 1892 these constituencies should have been changed by the Bill of that year.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: The redistribution of 1892 affected only two or three constituencies.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: I want to point out to the Committee and to my hon. friend that these differences did exist in 1892 and if the hon. gentlemen opposite applied the principle of representation by population when making changes in other places they should have made changes in these so that for purposes of illustration it is perfectly fair and right

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: Will the hon. minister give the names of these constituencies again ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: Simcoe, Toronto and York. I was showing that, although hon. gentlemen had departed from county boundaries and should have justly and fairly equalized the population according to the rule which they had declared was to govern them, these tremendous differences did exist.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: In other words there were sins of omission as well as sins of commission.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: I was going to discuss this matter with my hon. friend, not particularly from a party standpoint but advocating the principle of representation by population. I was pointing out on the other hand that we have adopted the principle of representation by county boundaries. That is the principle that we can discuss irrespective of any partisan feeling.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman give us the other constituencies ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext:
The three Yorks; the comparison clearly proves that the committee had not been

influenced by the suggestion made by Mr. McCarthy at that time, but that they endeavoured to stick as closely as possible, not only to the principle of county boundaries, but also to the equalization of population as far as possible. I believe that justification can be offered in every case for the differences in population that exist in the division within county boundaries. Every member of the House who takes an interest in the matter, knows that being limited to county boundaries it is quite likely there would be an inequality of population in some cases. Everything goes to show that although the Conservatives declared they went on the principle of representation by population, they departed from that principle and had no guiding rule. We all know the feeling that was aroused in this country at the great injustice done by the Conservative party in many Ontario constituencies, and we know that the people resented it by returning Liberals, although under normal conditions there was a large Conservative majority.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman seems to disregard that feeling now.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: On the contrary, we have endeavoured to redistribute the seats so that there would be no such feeling, and it is not enough for hon. gentlemen opposite to state in a general way, without giving proof, that any injustice has been committed. The people in these districts will pronounce that we have done what is fair and right under the circumstances.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: I ask the hon. gentleman if the plan submitted by the Liberal Association is not the plan now proposed by the majority of the committee. If it is changed in one iota he has made out a case ; if not, he has failed.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: As a member of that committee, I state here that I never saw that plan, and that I do not believe there was ever such a plan submitted to the committee by the Liberal Association. I do know that representations were made from different constituencies by party friends, but these representations were not adopted in many cases. The committee exercised its discretion to the best of its judgment, and in an impartial manner, and without partisanship. It is not sufficient now to get up a howl that injustice was done, without your being able to prove it. I deny that there is any injustice done. As a matter of fact, the Bill now before the House practically embodies the unanimous report of the committee, with the exception-

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: No, no.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext:
Will the hon. gentleman allow me to finish the sentence ? The Bill is practically the
unanimous report of the committee with the few exceptions which are to be found in the amendments submitted by the minority, and even in many of these amendments there is very little change suggested. I repeat that there is no material difference between the parties as to how the limitations of the ridings within the constituencies were to be made. It may be that the members of the committee made mistakes, but the members of that committee worked hard to ascertain what was fair and just under the circumstances, and they acted in that spirit. My hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker), well pointed out to-day, that if we were limited to county boundaries we had to consider other conditions than the equalization of population. I make this challenge, and I say that if you take the amendments submitted by the opposition, and take the proposals of this Bill ; the proposals in the Bill have more regard to the community of interests and to the geographical situation than have the amendments proposed by the opposition.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: That is a mere challenge, and the hon. gentleman knows it lias no foundation.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) knows very well, that I would not make the statement if I did not believe it to be correct. At all events, the facts are before the House and the country, and the people of the country can make the comparison for themselves. It is needless to point put that when the Conservatives were in power, they departed from the principles and rules which they now say should govern a redistribution measure. There was just as great a disparity in population an the divisions of the city of Toronto under the Conservative redistribution as there is under this. We give Toronto another member here.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: We gave them an extra member in 1892.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: It is too late at this stage to discuss the advisability of adopting county boundaries, but so far, no gentleman opposite has suggested any better principle accompanied by the proof that it is a better principle.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: Would it not be well for the hon. gentleman to take Mr. McCarthy's advice ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext:
I do not think so. I am proud to know that the members of that committee, and from the instructions of the government, did not take Mr. McCarthy's advice, but did the very opposite. They endeavoured to redistribute the seats fairly under the difficulties that existed. We had difficulties to face now that they had not in the former redistribution, because the fact that the representation of Ontario is cut

down from 92 to 86 has presented certain difficulties that did not exist then. That the county of Norfolk has lost a member, X am very sorry indeed, because it is one of the historic counties of Ontario, and I am quite sure that had it not been that we lost six members in Ontario the present representation of Norfolk would have been retained. No person has attempted to assert on the floor of this House that the rule adopted by the committee in applying the unit of population was not a fair rule, and under the application of that rule I regret to say that the county of Norfolk lost a member.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has two rules.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: It is all very well for the hon. gentleman to make these wild statements. We had not two rules. There were departures, as we have admitted, in two cases from the rule of county boundaries. These were thought to be in the public interest, as 1 stated before, and were agreed to unanimously by the committee, both sides being represented. If we had not desired to avoid any appearance of departing from the strict rule, I think that probably my hon. friend's proposition for equalization of population might have been earned out; but, as I pointed out on a previous occasion, the difficulty of departing from the rule that governed us was that it would have created further difficulties, because if it had been done in one case, it was natural to suppose that it would have had to be done in others. I think it would be far better and more in parliamentary form for us to take up the different counties and discuss the various propositions that have been made or that can be made in relation to them. Let the members point out any better way in which the committee could have divided any county; and if it can be shown, as the hon. gentleman asserts, that any injustice has been done, we will correct it. I am afraid that it is because he cannot point out any injustice that he makes these wild and extravagant statements about tire work having been done for party purposes. Let the hon. gentleman sit down and take the different counties and see whether or not, if we had adopted the various amendments submitted to the committee, greater injustice would not have been done to hon. gentlemen opposite from a party standpoint than is likely to be done by this Bill. If the hon. gentleman can give any good reasons why a change should be made in the case of any particular county, I for one would be perfectly willing to consent to it.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman should not say that the members representing the Conservatives asked for any departure from the rules. It is very astonishing Hon. Mr. SUTHERLAND.
to hear the hon. gentleman make that statement.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: I did not make that statement, so I have nothing to apologize for. I never made it on this occasion or on any previous occasion.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: I do not wish to do the hon. gentleman any injustice. I would be very sorry to accuse him of making a statement which he did not make. What I understood him to say was that if the rule had been followed, much greater injustice would have been done to the Conservative party than has been done. Did he say that ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: No, I did not say that. Neither did I say that the minority of the committee asked to have the rule violated. What I did say was that we did agree in one or two instances-to depart from the rule of county boundaries; but those departures were not forced on the minority of the committee, by any means. The hon. gentleman is altogether^ mistaken if he thinks that the committee were governed by any representations made by any committee of the Liberal party. I have stated-and I challenge any person to prove anything to the contrary- that no committee of the Liberal party ever at any time submitted, or attempted or offered to submit, any plan to the committee for the redistribution of seats in the province of Ontario. I want to disabuse the hon. gentleman's mind if he has been told that or has any such idea. Representations were made to the committee by both Conservative associations and Liberal associations, and these were considered and discussed in a very friendly and proper manner by the members of the committee representing both sides of this House; while many of the constituencies made no representations at all. I say again that we have to take the responsibility if we have done any injustice in regard to any of these constituencies, and it would be far better to discuss each one by itself, when the reasons could be given why we came to the conclusion we did, and when we could bear the reasons for any amendments that might be suggested. I think it will then be found that the committee, having heard all the suggestions and having given consideration to them, have come to a fair conclusion in submitting to the House the Bill in its present shape.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman began by saying that he was going to discuss this question free from partisan feeling; yet the very first thing he did was to give a quotation from a speech of the late Mr. Dalton McCarthy in 1892. Every hon. member who was a member of this House at that time knows perfectly well that Mr. McCarthy was not a supporter of the gov-

eminent, but (lid everything he could to injure the government.
An lion. MEMBER. Not in 1802.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: Yes, in 1892. I was in this House at that time, and I have the record in my hand to prove that statement. My hon. friend has quoted figures in respect to the redistribution of that year, and I infer from his remarks that he complained of that redistribution.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: No. I gave the constituencies as they stood, and showed that greater differences existed between constituencies under that redistribution than those which exist under tkfe present Bill.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: Then I take it that the hon. gentleman 1ms no fault to find with tlie redistribution of 1S92 ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: I have great fault to find with it.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: Is that because it did not go far enough or because it went too far?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: I was pointing out to the Committee that tlie bon. gentleman and his party are responsible, to a very great extent, for our having now to adopt some principle different from what was adopted at that time, on account of the great inequalities and injustices that existed.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext:
So, I take it that notwithstanding that the redistribution of the Conservative party in 1892 affected Only two or three constituencies, the hon. gentleman found fault with it because it was not more general. If that is the fault he finds witli it, he differs from his leader on that occasion; because his leader is on record as saying of the redistribution of 1892, on page 3118 of ' Hansard ' of that year :
Sir, this measure, which the Minister of Justice has professed to declare to be fair and equitable, I denounce to the House to-day, and in doing so I place myself in the judgment of the House, as an infamous attack on the minority, and I declare it to be an unmanly scheme in order to obtain by Legislation for the Conservative party seats which they would not be able to obtain by any other method. To characterize it as it should be characterized, there is no other term to apply to it hut the term from which the hon. minister himself recoiled, and to call it an odious gerrymander, and nothing else.
What did that infamous gerrymander do to the province of Ontario ? It gerrymandered a Conservative out of his seat in Monck. and a Liberal in Wentworth.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: What about the province of Quebec ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: I am not familiar with that province, but if there was any great hardship committed against it by the Conservative party, why does not my right hon. friend change it ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: That is what we are doing by this very Bill.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: There was no injustice done there or there would be some change made. A good deal has been said about 1892, but I think I remember a statement made by the former member for North Wellington, now Senator McMullen, some years ago, that in his opinion the redistribution of 1892 was a fair one.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: He never said anything of the kind.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: He was credited with having made that statement.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: I challenge the hon. gentleman to produce any such statement. The common opinion of the whole Liberal party was that it was a most infamous one.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: A most infamous measure.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: Yes, it was just an additional development of the crime of 1882. It was an outrage.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: Certainly it only affected two or three constituencies.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: It affected a great many.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: Can any hon. gentleman tell me where the iniquities appeared in 1892 ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: My hon. friend knows that in 1882 there was great indignation in this House and country over the Bill passed through parliament. In 1892 tlie late government had an opportunity to remedy that to a great extent, but they took no action in that respect, and my hon. friend knows that what action they did take with regard to two or three constituencies only added to the injustice done in 1882.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: Then it was because the Bill of 1892 did not go far enough that hon. gentlemen opposite complain.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: Both because of what it did and of what it did not.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext:
Now, I can get at what the Postmaster General means. He means that the Conservative party were to blame because the Redistribution Bill did not go far enough, and consequently there was wrong done in 1882. He maintains that there was wrong done in 1882 and that the redistribution of 1892 should have gone further than it did and should have undone the wrong it did in 1882. Hon. gentlemen opposite have quoted what the late Mr. McCarthy said in 1892 about tlie gerrymander of 1882; but if there was a man in this House then who deserved to be censured with respect to tlie redistribution of 1882,

it was the late member from Simeoe. He was the chief sinner. I would ash lion, gentlemen opposite if it was becoming in the chief sinner in 1882 to condemn in 1892 what he had done ten years previously ? Had the chief sinner the right to reprove others ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: Certainly.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: What was his motive 1

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: I do not know.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: It was the same as what lion, gentlemen opposite attribute to others.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: I do not think that my hon. friend ought to impute motives to a former member who is now deceased.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: That is perfectly true, but a number of hon. gentlemen on the other side have accused the late member from Simeoe with a desire to do injustice in 1882 to the Liberal party, and I am simply making the evident retort. I have no objection to hon. gentlemen opposite complaining about the redistribution of 1882, if they feel aggrieved, but when they describe the redistribution of 1892 as infamous, they are going too far, because it made scarcely any changes.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: The redistribution of 1892 reaffirmed that of 1882 and added to it.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: I am prepared to admit that in the matter of redistribution, other things being equal, the government should get the advantage, but I do not think they should go as far as they have gone in this Bill. They have gone entirely too far. I have listened to the arguments pro and con and have not heard of any particular rule being observed in the framing of this measure. I have shown what has been done in the counties of Brantford and Elgin. Take the county of Waterloo. My hon. friend the Minister of Customs (Hon. Mr. Paterson) talked about the county of Brant having been in a certain position for the last fifty years fcnd argued that on that account it ought not to be changed, but I did not hear him say a word in condemnation of the committee for making a change in the county of Waterloo, which was in a similar position for a similar length of time.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext:
What is the complaint about Waterloo ?
Mi-. INGRAM. My complaint is that for some fifty years it has been in a certain position and that the redistribution committee have changed that position without any justifiable reason. As regards population. the Minister of Justice the other day gave certain figures which were not correct.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: Let the hon. gentleman give the figures if he can.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman knows nothing about the redistribution at all outside the county of West York.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: Wait until you find out whether I know something about your county.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: I am not afraid of anything the hon. member can do, and am perfectly independent of him in every respect. I never had to take back anything I said yet.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: Well, you are squealing a great deal.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: I am not coward enough to deny being the father of any document.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: Take the medicine you gave to others.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: Hear, hear, order.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: I should be glad to sit down and let the hon. member take up the time of the House if he wants to, or let him cease his interruptions. What I have said about Waterloo I am prepared to prove, and that is that the change there is not for the purpose of equalizing the population, You have increased the difference by this change.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: We will discuss the reasons for the change when we come to Waterloo.

speechtext: We are discussing Norfolk, and a discussion on the division of Waterloo is out of order.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: But there is a distinction between a reference to AVater-loo and a discussion as to whether that county should be divided one way or the other. Reference can be made to it, but the propriety of dividing it or reuniting it cannot be discussed.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am drawing attention to the fact that in Brant and Waterloo practically the same conditions exist, and, while the hon. Minister of Customs upheld the division of Brant, he has not a word of condemnation when exactly the opposite course is followed with regard to Waterloo.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: I have not said anything yet.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: That is exactly what I am complaining of.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: Waterloo has not been under discussion.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext:
We have said that this committee was moved by no principle and governed by no rules, and that is what we find fault with. I have shown that that

which the minister condemns in the case of Brant he does not condemn in the case of Waterloo. There is no ground on which the thing can be justified. If the principle followed in the case of Brant were followed in the case of Waterloo, then Waterloo would be left untouched.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext:
I had not intended to say anything on this subject, but it is a little too much for human nature to stand to have lion, gentlemen opposite talking complacently, as they do, about the gerrymander of 1882, and comparing it with this Bill. Why, the measure of 1S82 was conceived in darkness and perpetrated in darkness. The government of that day brought their heelers from the different cities of Ontario, and, in darkness and in secret, they plotted in cold blood to take the political life of members of the opposition who were sitting with them in the House day by day, and with whom they kept up open- relations of friendliness. And when they thought they had succeeded, their press gloated over what they had done. For instance it was stated by the Conservative organ in Brantford with reference to myself, that the constituency now having been formed, ' We will have one last splutter from Paterson, and his light will go out.' That was the spirit in which it was done. Not a man in the opposition had any. knowledge of what was being done until the Bill was placed on the Table. And as the Liberals of that day looked at it, they saw the infamous attempt that was being made to take the political life of Alexander Mackenzie, of David Mills, of John Charlton, of myself-if I may include myself with these men-and many others. And the successors of the men wh6 were guilty of this crime rise here and denounce a Bill that lias been framed in the daylight, and the effect of which has been known to all the world. The hon. gentleman who last addressed us has himself told us that he was asked to come before the committee and give his views. Yet, these lion, gentlemen rise and propose, as this motion does, that county bounds shall be disregarded and the constituencies cut in part for special purposes. This the committee have not agreed to. They have been guided by principles which had been laid down in advance, and with which no fault can be found. Some Liberal members will lose their seats through this redistribution, just as some Conservative members will. But for an hon. gentleman to dare to bring forward a motion to justify their infamous political crime of 1882, surely cannot be considered without indignation. If any hon. gentleman thinks that by this Bill he has been personally struck at, let him fight. I shall not blame him. I fought. I did not whine-I fought. When I went home and was offered a safe constituency, I said ' No, I will stand by my own ; mangled as it is, I will try.' And there were enough decent Conservatives to
elect me, and it went on for a number of years that way. If there is a personal injustice done to any member of this House, as was done to so many of us in 1882, let that hon. gentleman take courage. He will come back here

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: He will not be helped by any excess of fairness on the hon. gentleman's (Hon. Mr. Paterson's) part.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, it is hard for any hon. gentleman who profited by the infamous gerrymander of 1882 to dare to say a word against this measure1-let him leave that to others. The Bill of 1882 was the most infamous gerrymander that ever was perpetrated. But, in the case of this Bill, did not the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy), who has interrupted me, have an opportunity to state his views to the committee 1

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: I was heard before the committee, and a deaf ear was turned to everything I had to offer, and to the statement of every principle of justice and fair-play.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: But the hon. gentleman was heard.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: That is where the mockery comes in.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: Mockery! When the proceedings of that committee went to the public through the press day by day ? If any injustice had been proposed, it would have been known to the world, and the press would have condemned it. Yet, I have not seen any paper that has felt it necessary to denounce any injustice under this measure. The abolition of Both-well, for instance, an electoral division made up of parts of several constituencies-does any body complain that these parts should go back "to the constituencies to which they belong ? If there is complaint of that in the press, I have not seen it.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: Have you read the Galt papers ? Galt is close to Brantford.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: No. I have not. Does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Ingram) who has interrupted me say that Bothwell should be retained as an electoral division ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: That is not the question.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: That is the very question. That is what the hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) denounces, yet the very gentleman (Mr. Ingram) who sits beside him will not venture to say that it is wrong.	[DOT]

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: I have answered the hon. gentleman's question.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: Yes, and just as I wanted it answered. What is being done in reference to Bothwell is something that ought to be done.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has misstated the whole thing.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: Let the hon. gentleman show how I have misstated it.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: I will tell the hon. gentleman. He said that there was no denunciation in the press of this redistribution scheme, and I asked him if he had read the Galt papers.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: And I said I had not. But I asked the hon. gentleman if he would say that Bothwell should continue to exist as an electoral district.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: Better ask my hon. friend (Mr. Clancy).

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: That is it. When these hon. gentlemen are asked to show where there is any injustice, their charge vanishes into thin ah'. I simply rose to contrast the Act that was perpetrated in darkness and in secrecy in 1882, when men were struck at deliberately and in cold blood, with this measure which has been discussed in open day-light, and the preparation of which was known to the world, so that if any injustice was contemplated it could be condemned. If there were injustice the public would condemn it. But where do we hear any condemnation to-day ? It is little less than an outrage that the time of his Committee should be occupied with these general charges, when we have before us a Bill with regard to which both sides have been able to agree except on certain points. And as to these points, we have tlie two propositions before us, and all we have to do is to discuss them. But that discussion cannot be promoted by mere vague and general charges of unfairness. The hon. gentleman says I did not speak about Waterloo. Waterloo was not under discussion. I spoke about Brant, it was under discussion. If I may say it to him, he will be unable to find any fault with Waterloo, because this afternoon he voted to take another part of a township that for fifty years has never cast its vote with South Brant and attach it to South Brant, while the portion that for fifty years has continuously voted with Brant should be thrown into another riding. That is what the hon. gentleman voted for this afternoon, and I suppose he cannot say that I am wrong in South Waterloo if there should be a change made there. I beg your pardon, Mr. Chairman, for taking up your time, but when they make an attempt to justify the gerrymander of 1882 I confess that I am hardly able to restrain myself, my indignation is too great. If I thought the party to which I belonged attempted or could attempt to act in that away, I do believe that I would leave it, for that iniquity of 1882 was burned so deeply into my soul that I have never been able to forget the perpetrators of it. It was a despicable

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: thing, in secret and in darkness, to plot the political assassination of men who were sitting opposite to them, with whom they professed to be, and were as members of the House, on friendly terms. I was pointing out where the inquiry, where the wickedness of that measure lay. It has been discussed in public, in daylight, discussed in the press, it is known to the people, it is before the House now in open daylight. Therefore it is for the House to pronounce and to judge, and it is about time we made some progress with the Bill.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: It is a great pity the hon. gentleman did not find that out before he madle ithis Violent harangue. The hon|. gentleman drops into extremes, he always does when he speaks of the redistribution of 1882. I never knew the hon. gentleman to be moderate, I never knew him to be more immoderate than to-night. The hon. gentleman knows that while there were six additional seats to be given to Ontario two by reason of wiping out Conservative constituencies in 1882 and four by reason of an increase of population, they were all given to Liberal counties, and in every case there was a Liberal elected at the next election.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: Was that the object of the gerrymander ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: I am pointing out the results. The hon. gentlemen are stating what the objects were, and I am pointing out what the results were, and I challenge the hon. gentleman to dispute the statement I have made.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman challenges me, I will refpl.v by giving the opinion which I read last night from an independent journal. In speaking of the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) it says :
We never heard that Mr. Henderson is crazy, but he compels suspicion.
So, any one that will begin to justify that iniquity of 1882 does not raise himself in the estimation of fair minded men.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: I presume it is many years ago that this House came to the conclusion that in certain cases the hon. member for Brant was worse than crazy, and if we have ever seen an exhibition of craziness-I do not want to use another word- I think we have seen it to-night. He has made an exhibition of craziness that I do not think I ever heard-come from any other man in this House, and I think hereafter he will be known as the crazy member for Brant. Now, I want to say just one or two words before I leave.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: Halton is not affected by this Bill.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext:
That is the reason, why I am going to speak. I am an unprejudiced witness in this case. I was not

affected in 1882 nor In 1893, and I am free therefore to express an unbiased opinion, and I am going to tell the crazy member from Brant

Some lion. MEMBERS. Order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has no right to apply the word ' crazy ' to another hon. member.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: All right, I accept you ruling, and I presume it applies to the hou. member for Brant as well.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext:
I did not say that the hon. gentleman was crazy,
I do not believe be is crazy, I do not think there is anything of that nature about him at all. I simply repeated what an independent paper said about him last night.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: I will say to the hon. gentleman that I did not think he was crazy enough to pay any attention to the statement he saw in the journal. I saw it, and it did not trouble me at all. I am going to say this to the hon. gentleman, and I say it in all sincerity, that the hon. member for Brant to-night is supporting a more unrighteous-I forget the word he used, it was something worse than that-a more unrighteous gerrymander than was ever perpetrated in this country or in any other country, as exhibited by the action of the government in the division of the county of Waterloo. It will go down to posterity, and the hou. gentleman will be charged as long as he lives with having done ail injustice to the Germans of North Waterloo and to the Scotch of South Waterloo. That is my JVonaSt conviction. The thou, gentlemlain may howl at the top of his voice, and try to drown his fears, or his sorrows, or his regrets, at the action taken, by making a boisterous noise. But I think he will always remember that he has do le something that he would rather have left undone.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman was not very courageous in quoting a statement from a newspaper of which he did not take the responsibility himself ? By quoting that statement from a newspaper in regard to my hon. friend from Halton he virtually adopted it as his own sentiment, but now he attempts to escape responsibility for it. Let me tell the hon. gentleman that all we see in print is not to be taken at its face value. It does not take much brains to write a squib of that kind. In nine cases out of ten when such extreme views are put forth, they are utterly worthless, and the man who writes them does not know anything about the situation. Now, I am going to read to the hon. gentleman the plan adopted by the Liberal leaders and by the Liberal Committee in reference to this redistribution. Here is a typewritten statement made on the 11th of May, 1903, before the Committee had held a single meeting. Here is what was framed by the Liberal party and worked
out, and not a change has been made in it to the extent of one ' i ' or one ' dot.' Does the hon. gentleman mean to say that this was a fair redistribution ? This plan was laid down, and I challenge the hon. gentleman to deny that it has been deviated from in one jot. Here is this typewritten statement made on the 11th of May last.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: Laid down by whom ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: Laid down by the Liberal committee.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: No, Sir.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext:
I will read it :
Proposed redistribution for Ontario. Submitted by Liberal members at an informal meeting on the 11th of May, 1903.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext:
I will read it through.
The boundaries of the territorial divisions mentioned in this scheme are those set forth in chapter 3 of the Revised Statutes of Ontario of 1897.
It goes on, and it names the identical constituencies that are to have turn members and those that are to have one member as stated in this Bill, irrespective of every consideration that might follow afterwards.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: That was not submitted by the Liberal committee. I am not responsible for the heading, but the truth is that the leader of the opposition, after considerable discussion in the committee, asked us to submit a statement in writing of what we thought would be a fair basis for redistribution. That was not submitted by some Liberal election committee, but by the members of the committee appointed by this House to consider the matter. The fact that there have not been many changes, proves that from the first we wanted to do what was fair and right ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has given a very lucid explanation.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: Is it not true ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman has made his case worse. This is a very important point. Whether inside or outside this House, the Liberals came to the conclusion that they would have a certain Bill, and they made this proposition on the 11th of May, before there was any open discussion in the committee, and that proposition has not been changed by this Bill in a single particular. The whole thing was cut and dried four months ago by the Liberals themselves. Will the hon. member (Hon. Mr. Paterson), who pumps up so much indignation on occasions of this kind, deny that ? If he is prepared to change his poli-

tical allegiance he will never have a better opportunity in his life, than to do so on a question of this kind. No Liberal or Conservative in Canada will believe that any political party would sit down and frame a Bill in the interest of both political parties. The government had the bad taste to invite Conservative members to sanction that prepared Bill, when there was no other course left open to them than to choose the lesser of two great evils. And yet we are told that no injustice was done. I will not discuss Bothwell to-night, as I understand there is an agreement about adjournment after certain items shall pass, but let me ask this : Was not the Hon. David Mills elected in 1882, and again in 1887, and again in 1891 ? The dispute now is not as to whether Bothwell will remain as it was before, but that the counties of Kent and Lambton shall be restored to their municipal boundaries. There is enough injustice done in the case of Bothwell to bring the blush of shame to the cheek of the hon. gentleman, if he has a blush left. I challenge him to deny my statement that this proposition was cut and dried on the 11th of May last by the Liberals on the committee. Of course with the concurrence and knowledge of their friends.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: How much of that proposition was afterwards agreed to by the committee ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: Let those answer who were present at the committee. The minority had to take this or worse. The Liberals held that they should have their Bill intact, and that if the Conservatives did not like it they would get something worse.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: It is refreshing to hear the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy), make such statements about the working of the committee. He says that the minority members on the committee were forced to accept the propositions of members on this side. How is it that they were not forced to accept the propositions, they were appealed against. They were forced to nothing. As an independent member of that committee

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: Hear. hear.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: Hon. gentlemen may say ' Hear, hear,' but as an independent member of that committee, and not knowing Ontario, I say that on the mere justice of the two propositions, and deciding on the arguments adduced, I would be forced to decide that the propositions of the Liberal members were the fairest and the most honourable. These gentlemen opposite gerrymandered the country some years ago, and they have forgotten that they have lost the power to gerrymander again. If some of the plans they submitted to the committee were adopted it would be a gerrymander indeed.
Item agreed to.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: 24-the territorial district of Nipissing.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: I wish to call attention to a representation which has been made to me since the report of the committee has come to the House. It is represented to me that the townships of Clara, Head and Maria have a population of 483. Under this Bill they are added to the constituency of Nipissing, but these three townships have always belonged to North Renfrew for all judicial purposes. They were added to Nipissing in 1901, under an Act of the legislature of Ontario, because it was intended to give to that electoral district two members instead of one. That has been represented to me as the reason for the adding of these three townships to that electoral district. But under the federal representation Act no such reason exists, because Nipissing is to have only one member. Now, Nipissing, as constituted by this Bill, would have a population of 36,551.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: No, my hon. friend is mistaken. The population, according to the census, is 28,309.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext:
The figure I have named has been given to me; but even taking the Sgure of the Minister of Public Works, the population of North Renfrew would be 24,558. Therefore, the reasons which existed for adding these three townships to Nipissing under the provincial statute do not exist here. These three townships belong to North Renfrew for judicial purposes, and it has been represented to me that there is no valid reason for adding them for electoral purposes to the county of Nipissing. As I may not be here when this subsection comes up for consideration, I would ask my right hon. friend to take this suggestion under advisement. I have communicated to my hon. friend the letter which I have received1 in reference to this proposed change, and I would like to lay before you, Mr. Chairman, a motion in these terms :
That the following words, after the word ' Nipissing,' in subsection 24, be omitted : * with the townships of Clara. Head and Maria.'
In order to make that amendment effective, I would move for the reconsideration of section 48, which I understand we have already adopted, and that the following words in that subsection be omitted ; ' exclusive of the townships of Clara. Head and Maria.' The object of these three motions is to leave these three townships in North Renfrew.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext:
I may say that the townships of Clara, Head and Maria lie along the Ottawa river, and they are geographically much better connected with Nipissing than they would be with Renfrew. They are not connected with Renfrew now for electoral purposes, and it would be against the wishes of the people, I understand, to so connect them. I

tliinlc my hon. friend from South Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart), who was a member of the committee for Ontario, will agree with that view, as he did in the committee. Originally, having a considerable settlement along the river, these townships were taken municipally into the county of Renfrew, For electoral purposes, both in the province and in the Dominion, they are now connected with Nipissing, and their people have petitioned the local legislature to add them municipally and judicially to that district. So that we would be doing a great injustice to these people to add those townships to North Renfrew against their wish. The matter lias no political significance; and if my hon. friend looks at the map, lie will see that they are closely connected with the more thickly part of Nipissing, while they are a long distance away from the main towns or settled parts of the county of Renfrew. It is the opinion, I think of the leaders of both parties from Ontario that they should remain as the Bill provides.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: Well, I deemed it my duty to bring this matter to the notice of the Committee, because the representation has been made to me since the committee sat. There is no political significance at all attached to this motion. The population of these three townships is given to me as 483, and I am informed that they are connected judicially with the county of Renfrew.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: Their petition has been before the provincial legislature, praying that they should be municipally and judicially connected with Nipissing. I understand that their prayer has not yet been granted, but there is no doubt that the Act will be passed in a few months.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: Of course, my hon. friend knows that in certain cases we have not adhered strictly to the rule which was laid down by the Prime Minister, and I am informed by a very respectable citizen of North Bay that the interests of these people lie in North Renfrew.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext:
That is a mistake, I am sure.
Mr. MACIvIE. The people living in these townships have applied to the Ontario government to have them connected with Nipissing. The Hon. Peter White had them added to North Renfrew in 1892.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: Are these townships not connected judicially with the county of Renfrew ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: They are, but they have appealed to the Ontario government to be added to Nipissing.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: Simply for the purpose of electing members for the local legislature.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: No. They are Liberal townships, and the Hon. Peter White applied to have them struck off in 1892.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: My hon. friend is, I think, mistaken when he says there is a political consideration in this matter, because the information which I have is that the voters in these townships are equally divided between the two parties, and my correspondent referred me to Mr. I'roulx, Mr. Champagne and Mr. Ethier to support this application, which he would not have done if there was any polities in the matter. At any rate, I place this application before the Committee. The population of Nipissing is greater by several thousands than that of North Renfrew, and therefore, if this application were granted, it would only have the effect of balancing the population.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: I think it is only necessary to look at the map to see that geographically these townships form a narrow fringe of country on the east side of Lake Nipissing, and they have very little if any geographical connection with Renfrew.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: I do not think my hon. friend has looked at the map lately.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext:
When we resume this discussion we will begin at Leeds, number 11, and will proceed by order on the

paper just as the items come. I suppose there will be no objection to that.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext: What day will we resume ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OP COMMONS.
speechtext:
As soon as we have disposed of the Grand Trunk Pacific Rajilway business, which will commence Monday morning.
Progress reported.
